Horrified at the Glazer family’s impending takeover two decades ago, a group of Manchester United fans went to church. FC United was their divine inspiration, a phoenix club born at the heart of the community

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Revolution can spark in the most unlikely places. John Lennon knew that. The former Beatle and wife Yoko Ono needed only an Amsterdam hotel room to stage their 1969 protest over the Vietnam War. Lennon’s decision to start a revolution from his bed would later be immortalised in the lyrics of Oasis’ Imagine pastiche Don’t Look Back in Anger.

Fully 36 years after that legendary ‘bed-in’, a group of football supporters chose an equally unlikely venue to kick-start their own revolution. Outraged by a hostile takeover of their beloved Manchester United, and fed up with where football appeared to be heading in general, they convened in May 2005 to discuss a notion that would send shockwaves through the English game. The meeting place: Methodist Central Hall in Manchester’s Northern Quarter.

“There was a buzz in the air,” explains Jules Spencer, a lifelong Manchester United fan who attended the event and had taken part in other protests. “We’d fought against change before, including Rupert Murdoch’s attempted takeover. But this was the final straw.”

Back in 1999, the United Kingdom’s Competition Commission had blocked Murdoch and BSkyB’s £625 million bid for Manchester United, the government’s reasoning that the acquisition would have “hurt competition in the broadcast industry and the quality of British football”. The next major power grab would not be so easily thwarted, though.

Malcolm Glazer, an American business tycoon and owner of NFL franchise the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, had first bought nearly three per cent of Manchester United in March 2003. Through a series of incremental buyouts, that stake neared 30 per cent by October 2004 – a threshold above which Glazer would have to launch a formal takeover bid.

Businessmen muscling into football was nothing new, but as the takeover drew nearer supporters became increasingly concerned. Most of the capital used by Glazer to buy the club would come in the form of loans, the majority of which were secured against the club’s assets, incurring average interest payments of more than £46m per annum.

“It was,” lifelong Red Devils fan Paul Hurst says, “absolutely scandalous.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In February 2005, hundreds of United fans protested outside Old Trafford, with some hanging an effigy of Glazer. That month, the idea for a breakaway club was first mooted by now defunct fanzine Red Issue.

“As the spectre of Malcolm Glazer looms ever larger, the question has been increasingly asked: ‘What would you do if he did take over?’” they penned. “What if you could give up supporting Glazer’s company without giving up United?

“Back in the days of the Murdoch campaign, an evacuation plan was drawn up, detailing the blueprint for the formation of a new Manchester United, one which spurned the commercialism and tackiness of the modern game, and was controlled and run by the fans. With United again under threat, those plans have been resurrected. With a working name of ‘FC United’, the logistics of the operation to set up a new Manchester United has been looked into.”

The article outlined the bold ambition. “We would await regime change, while aiding all attempts to undermine the illegitimate occupation,” it continued. “When Glazer is defeated, FC United will be happy to return to Old Trafford and merge with ‘the franchise’ on condition that the supporters’ trust maintains full ownership of the football club and the unified Manchester United take over the higher league position of FC United. Viva la revolucion.”

Three months later, Glazer completed his takeover, reaching the 75 per cent threshold required to end the club’s public limited company (PLC) status and delist from the London Stock Exchange.

It prompted fans to assemble and discuss a new club at Methodist Central Hall, complete with Styrofoam cups of tea in hand, surrounded by murals of Bible scenes and psalms.

“I’d taken part in the protests against the Glazers, along with so many others,” says Hurst, who was at that meeting. “Many of us pledged not to give the club one penny more while Glazer owned it. We wouldn’t be paying off his debts.”

“It wasn’t about switching off our allegiance to Manchester United – that would never go,” remembers Spencer. “It was about letting Manchester United and the Glazers know that we wouldn’t stand idly by and allow this to happen. If necessary, we were willing to put our money towards something else instead, something positive to be proud of.”

Red Issue editor John-Paul O’Neill organised the new movement, backed by a steering committee. “It was drawn from across the fanbase, from official fan groups to business people and those with marketing and communications expertise,” says team member Spencer. “We held more meetings, with around 1,500 people joining at Manchester’s Apollo theatre. Not everybody was convinced, but they came along to hear what we had to say. Momentum began to build and some fans started to pledge their United season ticket money to help us get off the ground. It was so exciting.”

Preparations included a visit from Kris Stewart, chairman of AFC Wimbledon, founded three years earlier. “His insight was invaluable,” recalls Spencer. “We didn’t really know what we were doing at that stage. He told us we were in for a lot of hard work and that a lot would go wrong, but it’d be totally worth it if we pulled it off. He remained a valued sounding board in the months to come.”

Time was of the essence. The new club had to be set up and registered well before the new 2005-06 season, already less than two months away. Failing to do so would risk losing momentum. They didn’t even have a name.

The FA vetoed ‘FC United’ for being too generic, so those who’d pledged money were asked to vote on a different name. Manchester Central and Newton Heath United were discarded as options – in June, ‘FC United of Manchester’ got the nod and joined the 10th-tier North West Counties Division Two. While it wasn’t their official moniker, many called them FC United anyway

There was still the not insignificant issue of finding some players. Some 900 applications were whittled down to 200 trialists, from which Karl Marginson, the club’s inaugural manager, would select a squad of 17.

“The standard of the trialists was very strong and we put together a team I felt capable of challenging for the title in our first campaign,” he tells FFT now.

How did the manager get the gig? “It was between me and one other bloke, and he was a Scouser,” Marginson, a born-and-bred Manc chuckles. “I was 34 – I’d been an assistant at Flixton, so not had a proper manager’s job before, but I knew the league well.

“I’d been a Manchester United fan all my life and didn’t like where the original club was heading. I didn’t think my own kids would be able to afford to go when they were old enough, the way I had as a teenager, and that was so wrong. The new club was important and I think they could see what it meant to me as well. I was young and ambitious – the idea of taking charge of a totally new club appealed to me.”

Their first match was a drab 0-0 draw at Leigh RMI. The pre-season friendly was watched by more than 2,500 fans, TV crews and national journalists. “It was magnificent and bonkers at the same time,” says Marginson. “There was a party atmosphere in the air, even for such a terrible game. I couldn’t believe what I’d let myself in for.”

A similar-sized crowd flocked to FC United’s first competitive match, a 5-2 victory at Leek County School Old Boys, whose ground was used to hosting fans by the dozen, not the thousand. Home matches, staged at Bury’s Gigg Lane as part of a long-term groundsharing deal, delivered gates as large as 6,000 during a season that consistently smashed the league’s attendance records.

“It was incredible to see,” reminisces future board member Hurst. “The level of football was very different to what we’d been used to, nine divisions higher in the Premier League, but the sense of community more than made up for it.”

The matchday mood wasn’t always positive, though. Throughout the club’s formation, a small yet vocal group of Manchester United supporters had railed against the movement, branding those involved traitors. Tensions flared during a game against Salford City. “The fixture had to be switched to Salford’s rugby league ground due to the expected crowd,” explains Hurst.

“Lots of Manchester United fans bought tickets to protest against us, which was ironic. They had some banners calling us turncoats and all the rest of it. It got quite unpleasant.”

Even Sir Alex Ferguson weighed in on the new club, labelling the movement “a shame” and questioning whether those involved were really proper Red Devils to begin with.

“Listen, we could all understand the criticism to a certain degree,” continues Hurst. “The new club was divisive, even within families and friendship circles.

“There were those that saw it as the genuine protest movement it was – a necessary act of defiance – and others who saw us as Judases who turned our back on the club in its hour of need. That was never the case.

“Many of us are passionate Manchester United supporters. We just didn’t want to fund Glazer’s debts by going to games. Thankfully, a lot of that hatred has died down since.”

On-field headlines were positive. The Red Rebels swept to the Division Two title in their first season, finishing eight points clear of Marginson’s former club Flixton. “A fantastic achievement,” he says. “It was important to show that we were a club that meant business in footballing terms as well, beyond the protest club element.”

They were far from done. FC United won promotion again in their second campaign, then another in their third to reach the Northern Premier Division, two levels below the National League and three from the EFL.

A fourth promotion was squandered in 2010-11, courtesy of a play-off final defeat to Colwyn Bay. Earlier in that season, FC United had advanced to the FA Cup first round for the first time, then won at League One Rochdale to set up a second round showdown at Brighton, who would go on to win the third tier that term.

The 10-man Red Rebels even led at the Withdean Stadium, before Mauricio Taricco’s late equaliser earned Gus Poyet’s Seagulls a replay they would win 4-0 at Gigg Lane. The 6,900 gate that night was more than 1,500 higher than the first encounter in East Sussex.

Further play-off defeats followed in 2012, 2013 and 2014. “I definitely felt the pressure to win matches and keep taking the football club forward,” says Marginson. “I was still inexperienced and we were getting huge attendances to every game.

“We had one of the bigger budgets in those leagues and supporters expected a lot. I already drank alcohol, but I’d be lying if I said I didn’t lean into that a bit more to help cope.”

Promotion eventually came in 2015 – not only did FC United secure a fifth successive top-six finish, this time they won the league, during a campaign in which they groundshared with Curzon Ashton and Stalybridge Celtic. “It was an epic achievement,” says Marginson with pride. “The club stuck by me and we got there in the end.”

The timing couldn’t have been better, with a new 4,700-capacity home all of their own ready to move into.

“Gigg Lane served us incredibly well, but financially it made more sense for us to have somewhere permanent,” says director Hurst. “We scouted out a number of sites before the council let us build a new stadium in Moston.”

Located just four miles north-east of Manchester city centre, Broadhurst Park cost £6.5m and hosted its first match, a friendly against Benfica B, on May 29 that year – the same date on which Manchester United beat Benfica in the 1968 European Cup Final. “It felt like a massive step for us,” adds Spencer. “A place to stand with our friends, our sons and daughters, and call home.”

FC United finished a respectable 13th in the National League North on two occasions, but a tough start to 2017-18 resulted in Marginson’s exit. “If you’d have told me when I first took the job that I’d still have been there all those years later, I’d have said, ‘No chance’,” he says, reflecting on 12 years in charge. “I think back to the young man I was when I became manager – it’s a world apart. I couldn’t have done the job had I been older. It needed youth and energy from the off. Eventually, I ran out.”

A new injection arrived in the form of striker Tom Greaves – the club’s all-time top scorer – who stepped up to a player-manager role. He steered the club to survival but departed after a poor start to the next campaign, to be replaced by Neil Reynolds. He, though, couldn’t turn the tide, with FC United relegated back to the Northern Premier Division. COVID annulled 2019-20 when they were sat second and set for the play-offs again – five years on, they’re yet to return to the sixth tier of the pyramid.

Not that it’s all been doom and gloom. Later in 2020, FC United reached the FA Cup first round for the third time, facing League One Doncaster Rovers in front of the live TV cameras. A year after that, they were invited to participate in the inaugural Fenix Trophy, a tournament contested by a selection of unusual non-league sides from across Europe. The Mancunians travelled to face AKS Zly in Warsaw, and Brera in Milan, going on to beat Prague Raptors in the final in the Italian city of Rimini.

In 2022-23, they again reached the latter stages of the competition, losing a semi to BK Skjold of Denmark but then beating Brera at Milan’s San Siro, no less. Last season, after matches in Krakow and Paris, they won the cup for a second time, defeating Prague Raptors in the final once more, on the shores of Lake Garda on this occasion.

“I certainly didn’t envisage leading my team-mates out at San Siro when I first joined,” says club captain Charlie Ennis, who arrived in the summer of 2019. “Getting changed in Milan’s dressing room and walking out onto that iconic pitch – it still gives me goosebumps now. We’ve been very lucky to be a part of the competition, travelling across Europe. It’s been one of the highlights of my career.”

Ennis, now 34, is another who didn’t expect to stay as long as he has. “I was no spring chicken when I signed,” he jokes. “But I’m a local lad and, short of playing for Manchester United, who I grew up supporting, there’s nowhere else I’d rather be. We get big crowds, play at a fantastic ground and this club means so much to people. The best years are yet to come.”

The man tasked with leading them into the next era is gaffer Mark Beesley, who replaced Reynolds in September after resigning from Warrington Town. His squad includes 38-year-old former Reading and Bolton forward Adam Le Fondre, a lifelong Manchester United fan who spoke of semi-fulfilling a dream when signing from Scottish Premiership side Hibernian last summer.

Whatever the future holds, FC United can already look back on the past two decades with enormous pride. “It’s been a lot of hard work, but I wouldn’t have changed it for the world,” director Hurst tells FFT now. “You look over at Manchester United, what continues to happen at the club with its ownership, and you’d be hard pressed to say we were wrong to do this. We’ve given local football fans a positive alternative.”

Manchester United are still majority-owned by the Glazers. Malcolm passed the reins to his sons before his death in 2014. Since the family took charge, it’s estimated the club has paid out more than £750m in interest fees on loan repayments alone. Debts remain high, while on-field success has steadily declined since Ferguson’s retirement. Ineos impresario Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s £1bn investment for a 27.7 per cent stake has rekindled neither success nor spirit.

“We want more than anything for that to change, for the Glazers to sell up, and for Manchester United to become a well-run club again,” says Spencer. “I’m still a Manchester United fan. I was jumping for joy when we beat City in last season’s FA Cup final. But as long as the Glazers are still there, I can’t be.”

Until that day, and long after, Spencer and his fellow rebels will be found at Broadhurst Park. “I come here with my sons and it’s a special feeling,” he says. “It’s something positive that we can all share as a community. I look back at that meeting at the church hall all those years ago and can’t help but laugh at how far we’ve come since. We made the right decision.

Ed is a staff writer at FourFourTwo, working across the magazine and website. A German speaker, he’s been working as a football reporter in Berlin since 2015, predominantly covering the Bundesliga and Germany's national team. Favourite FFT features include an exclusive interview with Jude Bellingham following the youngster’s move to Borussia Dortmund in 2020, a history of the Berlin Derby since the fall of the Wall and a celebration of Kevin Keegan’s playing career.

The Celtic great moved south of the border in 1977

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When Kenny Dalglish arrived at Liverpool from Celtic in 1977, he arrived as a 26-year-old, just entering his peak years.

Signed as a replacement for Hamburg-bound Kop icon Kevin Keegan, Dalglish eclipsed even King Kev’s achievements in Reds shirt over the next decade and a half.

But the Scot’s move to Anfield almost happened a decade earlier, when he was still a teenager.

“Myself and another boy were invited for trials with Liverpool when I was a teenager,” Dalglish tells FourFourTwo. “We played a game, then I was asked to go back for a couple of weeks.

“Shanks [Billy Shankly] was there, I played a game and they said. ‘We'd like to sign you.' I thought, ‘It's a bit far from Glasgow…' I knew that Liverpool was a great club, I just thought it was too far away for a 15-year-old boy going down there by himself.”

Dalglish would go on to become a Celtic great, winning four Scottish league titles and four Scottish Cups before Liverpool came knocking again.

“Then in 1977, when I was 26, I'd been in South America for World Cup warm-ups with Scotland, because the World Cup was going to be in Argentina the next year,” he recalls.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I came home, Celtic were going to Australia and I said to the manager, ‘I don't want to go.' Jock Stein said, ‘Go home and think about it.'

“I told him, ‘I have thought about it', and by the way, for me to stand up to him like that, I was terrified! I stayed at Celtic Park and trained with the reserves.

What followed next was a clear sign that Stein was preparing for life without his star player.

“When the first team came back, I played a couple of pre-season games, one at Dunfermline. We were in the dressing room, ready to go out and I was captain, but Big Jock threw the ball at one of the other players and said, ‘On you go, you take them out.'

“The rest of them were all saying to me, ‘Oh… where are *you* going?' I said, ‘I don't know!' “After the game, I dropped into my father-in-law's pub on the way home. Big Jock phoned the pub and said, ‘Right, do you still want to go?' I said, ‘Aye, boss.' He said, ‘Get yourself up here, there are two people who want to talk to you.'

“It was about 10.30pm – Bob Paisley and the chairman of Liverpool were there. About five minutes later, everything was agreed.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#821. The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.

This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.

But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.

While the other regional champions in the German fourth division were promoted to the nationwide 3. Liga, "Lok" faced a play-off against a representative of the Regional League Bavaria, Wurzburger Kickers. Ziane scored, but an injury-ravaged Leipzig lost 3-1 on aggregate.

"Euer System ist krank," read a simple protest banner displayed by the 2,000 travelling supporters â "your system is sick".

"It's the worst thing â injury aside â that you can experience as a footballer," Ziane tells BBC Sport.

"Catastrophe doesn't cut it. It doesn't make any sense. If they really wanted to change it, they could do tomorrow."

A banner reading 'Your system is sick' was displayed at this year's promotion play-off

Germany's football pyramid has a bottleneck.

Beneath the Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga, the fourth tier is split into five regional divisions (North, West, Southwest, Northeast and Bavaria), each of which produces a league champion.

So far, so good. But with only four teams being relegated from the 3. Liga each season, the sums don't add up.

An unsatisfactory solution is currently in place: the champions in the West and Southwest go up automatically while a third automatic promotion spot is rotated among the other three leagues in a three-year cycle. The fourth spot is allocated via a play-off between the winners of the remaining two leagues.

One champion always misses out and, increasingly, it's the champion from the Regional League Northeast, covering the territory of the former eastern German Democratic Republic (GDR).

In addition to Lok Leipzig's triple tragedy, former serial GDR Oberliga winners Dynamo Berlin fell short in 2022 and Energie Cottbus drew the short straw in 2023. This season, there is only one eastern German club in the 3. Liga: Hansa Rostock.

The struggles of the regions' football clubs are, to some degree, a result of continuing socio-economic disparities between east and west, which were also reflected in the success of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in recent state elections.

Even in 2026, not one of the 40 leading companies listed on Germany's DAX stock exchange is based in the former east (outside Berlin). Salaries remain lower, unemployment remains higher and the population is older and shrinking as young people move west.

The reason that automatic promotion spots are handed to the champions in the West and Southwest is simply because there are more men's football teams registered in those jurisdictions - because more people live there.

It is an argument that Ziane is tired of hearing.

"In that case, you might as well give us the automatic promotion spot because we attract bigger crowds," he says.

Indeed, the average attendance in the Regional League Northeast last season (3,125) was around twice as high as that in the other leagues. Lok Leipzig themselves had the fourth highest (6,352). More than 11,000 attended the local derby against city rivals Chemie Leipzig.

"Unfortunately, you don't get any points for tradition, crowds and history," says 39-year-old Lok chief executive Toni Wachsmuth, who does not have access to sponsors with the same financial firepower as his counterparts further west.

"The [western] leagues do have better economic foundations but everyone agrees that the current system is nonsense. Everyone needs to compromise but some officials are clearly putting their own interests and positions above the general good of German football."

It comes as little surprise, therefore, that the latest push for change has come from the east, with clubs launching a new campaign in March 2025 with the slogan: "Meister mussen aufsteigen!" â champions must go up!

Their proposal: a reduction from five leagues to four, with the precise geographical borders to be determined anew each season with the help of artificial intelligence, taking into account factors such as distance of travel to away games and attractive derbies.

They call it the compass model. Because it can go in all directions. In return, the Regional League Northeast is prepared to compromise by giving up its emotional attachment to the territory of the former East Germany.

"I want to get away from this east-west debate," says Tommy Haeder, the 35-year-old chief executive of Chemnitzer FC and figurehead of the reform campaign. "We've had a change of generation. Many older officials have retired and been replaced by younger people who don't have this nostalgia for the GDR."

Haeder also emphasises the benefits that a fairer promotion system would bring for German football as a whole, arguing that eastern clubs would be better equipped to continue nurturing youth talent.

"It's not in the interest of talent development when young footballers from Chemnitz are torn away from their homes and families at the age of 10 to join academies in Hamburg, Dortmund or Stuttgart," he tells BBC Sport.

"The compass model is a model in which every region sacrifices a little bit to solve a much bigger problem. We're organised, we have a plan, we've made suggestions. Now it's up to the federations to act."

The campaign has since gained the support of more than 80 clubs across Germany, from east to west and up and down the pyramid.

Union Berlin, who were playing in the fourth tier as recently as the 2000s, became the first Bundesliga club to officially back the initiative, with club president Dirk Zingler saying: "The current set-up contradicts our understanding of sporting competition."

Borussia Dortmund president â and Bundesliga chairman â Hans-Joachim Watzke added his influential voice, stating: "Champions must go up and we think the compass model with four regional leagues is the best option."

Support also has also come from Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose who, drawing on his past as both a player and coach at Lok Leipzig, said: "I know what it's like for clubs trying to work within their means, or lack of means, at that level. Everything is on a knife edge.

"You have to give the clubs and their fans the belief that their efforts and sacrifices will be rewarded with promotion."

Momentum was growing before a key vote at the end of June when, after months of discussions, clubs were finally set to vote on the compass model â but the ballot descended into farce when, at the last minute, the regional federations conducting the vote announced two key changes:

Suddenly, the four new leagues would consist of only 18 teams rather than 20 (thus making the compass model less attractive because 10 more teams would miss out), and a stipulation was added that a majority be reached in each of the five regions for the model to pass.

An overall majority (50.9%) in favour of the compass model was still reached (including 60.9% in the West, 61.5% in the North and 76.3% in the Northeast) but the Southwest voted for an alternative option in which the northeastern league would be dissolved and its clubs reallocated, while the Southwest and West would simply remain the same.

"The move from a functioning system to a complex, insecure and economically riskier model without an obvious benefit doesn't make any sense to me," Robert Lempka, chief executive of Regional League Southwest side FSV Frankfurt told local public broadcaster Hessischer Rundfunk this summer. "I find it unsettling that an untransparent algorithm should decide a club's future."

The Bavarians, meanwhile, voted vaguely for "further talks", with Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) President Christoph Kern telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper in August: "We've gathered our clubs together on several occasions and none of the suggested models have majority support. I'm not prepared to simply give up the Regional League Bavaria like that."

For Haeder in Chemnitz, the vote was "an absolute catastrophe â completely amateurish". And he's not alone.

This season, protests have erupted across German football. In the Regional League Northeast, almost every game has begun with a delay as players have simply refused to play for the first minute.

On the opening day, Lok Leipzig supporters, their team still stranded in the same division, threw hundreds of plastic trophies on to the pitch, symbolising the worthlessness of their club's back-to-back titles.

Down in Bavaria, Bayern Munich's ultras attended a reserve team game in the regional league and produced an intricate choreography criticising the Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) for what they perceive to be an unco-operative stance.

"You've taken us for fools long enough," read a banner beneath a display depicting BFV officials using a magnet to pull a compass needle towards them. The ultras then set off red pyrotechnics which turned the compass needle back in the direction of the fans.

And before the international break, fans of clubs across the Bundesliga used their platform to call for reform with co-ordinated banners reading: "Clubs and fans betrayed! Champions must go up! Compass model now!"

The compass, it would appear, may finally be pointing towards a resolution after the German Football Federation (DFB) announced the convening of an extraordinary general meeting on 18 December.

"[The issue] must be resolved," said President Bernd Neuendorf. "The compass model received the most votes and offers the best chance for a concentration of elite performance and therefore better development of talent."

Any changes would only be implemented in the 2028-29 season â too late for Ziane who, now 34, has embarked on his 13th season with Lok Leipzig. Back-to-back champions, but still in the fourth division.

"You can never completely get over it because, at our level, the 3. Liga is probably the pinnacle. Promotion with my hometown club would have been the most wonderful thing in the world for me," he says before heading out for training.

"It's a shame that we have to force ourselves to remember what we've achieved. It's so hard to win this league and we did it twice in a row! You can't take that for granted."

Former world No 1 Jannik Sinner is set to undergo surgery on his troublesome knee which is likely to see him miss the Australian Open in January, according to Sky in Italy.

The surgery, performed by Lasse Lempainen, one of the world's leading specialists in tendon and muscle injuries, could sideline the Italian for three to four months.

The 25-year-old stated earlier this month that he expects to make his official return at the Australian Open following a planned appearance at the Six Kings Slam in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in late December.

"The goal is to go to ​Australia; I hope to get there, and perhaps play a few tournaments beforehand," Sinner told media in Milan.

Despite playing only nine tournaments, Sinner compiled an astonishing 44-3 match record (93.6 per cent win rate), where he captured six titles and reclaimed the world No 1 spot during a 30-match winning streak.

He sealed maiden titles in Indian Wells, Monte-Carlo, and Madrid to become only the second man in history [after Novak Djokovic] to win all nine ATP Masters 1000 tournaments.

However, Sinner did not feature in another competitive match after beating Alexander Zverev in four sets to secure his second consecutive Wimbledon title in July, with persistent inflammation in his right knee forcing him to miss the North American hard-court swing, including the US Open.

Rushden was a TV newcomer when he landed the top job on Sky’s iconic football show

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For a generation of football fans in the UK, Soccer AM was a staple of their Saturday morning routine.

The Sky TV show combined football, comedy and celebrity guests, all with a healthy dose of general chaos.

When TV newcomer and longtime Soccer AM fan Max Rushden landed the co-presenter job alongside Helen Chamberlain in 2008, he was thrown into a world he had never experienced before.

“Getting the job was mad because I'd never done a TV show in my life, and it definitely showed in the first two years,” Rushden tells FourFourTwo.

“But I loved the show – I was a fan of the week in 2000 and watched it religiously until about two or three years before getting the job, so the whole thing was surreal.”

Rushden’s journey from avid viewer to presenter had plenty of twists, including an audition for another iconic British TV programme.

“I was doing a breakfast show on Radio London, but I had to go back to reading the news because I wasn't famous,” he continues.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I thought, ‘OK, I'll make a show and send it to everybody' – the only two people who replied were from the Travel Channel, who said I was boring, and Sky Sports, who asked me to go in for a chat.

“I bowled in, chatted about Cambridge and Soccer AM for an hour. They said they might have something for me in a couple of months, but I didn't expect much.”

After leaving the audition with low expectations, Rushden continued to explore other possibilities.

“In the meantime, I'd got an audition for Blue Peter,” he reveals before receiving a life-changing telephone call.

“Before I went to it, I got a call from Sky and they asked, “Do you want to do Soccer AM?” My head just exploded and I was trying to play it cool.

"I signed the contract and s**t myself for a month before the show started.”

#817. Mustaki out of World Cup play-off with knee injury

Chloe Mustaki is a key figure for Carla Ward's Republic of Ireland side

Republic of Ireland defender Chloe Mustaki has been forced to withdraw from her side's 2027 Women's World Cup play-off final against Poland next month after rupturing her anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

The 31-year-old sustained the injury in action for Nottingham Forest against Liverpool in the League Cup last week.

Her club have confirmed the centre-back will miss the rest of the season and that their medical team will "determine the best course of action for her rehabilitation and recovery".

Republic of Ireland manager Carla Ward said she was "absolutely devastated" for the player who will be a huge loss in the side's efforts to make it the tournament in Brazil next summer.

She added: "It is a huge blow for the entire squad because of how important she is to this group, both on the pitch with her consistency and leadership, and off the pitch with the incredible character and positivity she brings to the dressing room.

"This is a really difficult setback, but Chloe is loved by us all. Everyone in the squad, the staff and the association is fully behind her, and we will give her all the love and support she needs to make a full recovery."

Ward will not call up a replacement to her squad with the 24-player panel set to gather in Dublin on Tuesday.

They will play the first leg of the play-off in Gdansk on 1 December with the return fixture at the Aviva Stadium four days later. Both games kick off at 17:00 GMT.

#816. Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy

Abortion laws in Poland are very restrictive. Activists there have found a new way to help women wanting to terminate a pregnancy: the "Abortomat," a locker that dispenses abortion pills. But they face fierce opposition.

Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.

Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.

In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

The "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.

Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.

"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.

Women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.

In 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.

Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.

Dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, said the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated."

She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.

"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she said.

The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," said Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.

At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan."

"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she said.

Earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.

Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.

"I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she said.

"I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.

In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.

Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

"I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she said.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.

In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.

The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.

Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents said they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.

Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

Martin Bakole will replace Jai Opetaia and fight Deontay Wilder on the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua undercard at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on December 11; Bakole lost to Joseph Parker at short notice and has scored outstanding wins over Tony Yoka, Carlos Takam and Jared Anderson

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Martin Bakole will fight Deontay Wilder on the undercard of Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua on December 11.

Fury and Joshua finally meet after a long-running rivalry in the main event at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff.

Wilder is a former WBC heavyweight world champion renowned as one of the hardest punchers in the sport.

He was due to box Australian cruiserweight star Jai Opetaia, who withdrew injured and will now remain in the 200lb division.

"Bakole is next, and then after that, it's going to be crazy," Wilder said in a post by @heavyweighttruth on Instagram.

"I ain't going to move forward with the information that I've received, but once I beat him, you're looking at the new heavyweight champion of the world.

"Martin, here we come, baby. I appreciate you for accepting the opportunity, and let's give the fans, let's give the people something to talk about for the rest of their lives."

Bakole was already scheduled to box on the card and is no stranger to taking a big fight on short notice. He travelled at just three days' notice to step in for Daniel Dubois and box Joseph Parker.

Prior to that Bakole scored outstanding wins over Tony Yoka, Carlos Takam and elite American hope Jared Anderson.

"Wilder and Bakole have 66 wins and 59 knockouts, so you don't want to miss this fight."

Welsh heavyweight Moses Jolly also joins the card in a bout against Igor Adiel Macedo with more bouts still to be announced.

#813. Is trust in science falling, or does it just feel that way?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Linda Nordling is a freelance journalist in Cape Town, South Africa.

This article is the third in a series discussing the results of Nature’s 2026 science-job satisfaction survey. It’s the latest edition of such surveys, which started in 2010; the last two took place in 2018 and 2021. The 2026 survey, created in partnership with Thinks Insight & Strategy, a research consultancy in London, launched in May and was advertised on nature.com, in Springer Nature digital products and through e-mail campaigns. It had 3,882 self-selecting respondents across 133 countries with 31% describing themselves as female and 19% as belonging to a minority ethnic group in their country of work. The full survey data sets are available at go.nature.com/4b2drrc.

Iris Borowy thinks that teaching her postgraduate students how to tell fact from fiction is central to her job. Yet some days, that work seems futile. “I feel silly teaching groups of eight people while, out there in the influencer sphere, complete idiots talk to millions,” says Borowy, a global-development historian at Shanghai University in China. “Granted, there are a lot of serious people doing good work online, but working against the propaganda is getting harder.”

Borowy is one of the researchers who told a Nature survey earlier this year that they felt public trust in science had declined over the previous five years. Of around 3,900 respondents, 50% shared this view, with 33% thinking that trust had increased and 13% saying that it had stayed the same (see ‘Perceptions versus reality of public trust in science’).

Even though trust in science remains high overall, data from other surveys support the idea that trust levels have fallen slightly, after rising at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. A global survey of more than 140,000 people in 140 nations, published in October by the London-based funding charity Wellcome, found that the proportion of the public who trust science “a lot” or “some” declined from 80% in 2020 to 72% in 2025. Trust levels dropped below pre-pandemic levels in 5 of 14 regions: Australia and New Zealand, sub-Saharan Africa and central, western and eastern Asia. It rose in just two areas — western and southern Europe. In seven regions, including North America and northern Europe, it remained close to the 2018 pre-pandemic levels, when 77% of overall respondents expressed trust in science.

Nature’s survey data — which measure scientists’ perceptions of changes in public trust levels, not trust levels themselves — only partly match the trends in the Wellcome survey. In our self-selecting survey, respondents in Africa and Asia were the least likely to say that trust in science had dropped (28% and 34%, respectively). By contrast, 78% of respondents in North America and 64% in Europe thought that public trust had declined. Nature’s survey also revealed that perceptions of falling public trust colour scientists’ job satisfaction and influence who they think is ultimately responsible for rebuilding trust.

How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts

How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts

The mismatch between actual trust levels in North America and Europe, which remain relatively high, and some scientists’ impression that they’re markedly declining could be explained by a few things, says Niels Mede, a science-communication researcher at Wageningen University in the Netherlands. One is that people who don’t trust science have become louder and more visible, particularly online, and that their messaging is making scientists feel threatened. This has driven a narrative in science media and policy debates of a “crisis of trust”, he says, which has fuelled the perception that overall trust is going down. In addition, he says, many scientists hold a pessimistic view of the public — seeing lay audiences as uninterested in and apathetic to science.

There is also strong evidence that, in countries where scientists told Nature they felt trust in science had dropped, opinions about science are becoming more polarized along political lines. This is especially visible in the United States, where trust among right-leaning Republicans dropped sharply after the COVID-19 pandemic, whereas trust among left-leaning Democrats remained high. In the Netherlands, trust in science remains high overall but the proportion expressing low trust grew from 9.5% in 2019 to 14.6% in 2025. A UK survey published in April found that the proportion who trusted science “a lot” had dropped from 63% in 2020 to just 34%.

Given the gap between perceptions and realities when it comes to public trust of science, Mede says that it’s important to read the trends in Nature’s survey “as a measure of how scientists experience their relationship with the public, not as a measure of public trust per se”.

Digging down into the country-level data from the Nature survey, it is clear that there are big geographical differences in scientists’ perceptions of public trust.

In the United States, 83% of respondents felt that trust in science had decreased in the past five years, compared with 79% in Germany and 78% in the United Kingdom. By contrast, just 23% of respondents in India reported feeling that public trust in science had decreased, with a considerable majority — 61% — saying that they felt it had increased. In Japan, 37% of respondents felt trust in science has decreased, whereas 38% said it has stayed the same.

What’s the secret sauce for happy scientists at work? These eight countries offer some clues

What’s the secret sauce for happy scientists at work? These eight countries offer some clues

Nature’s findings from respondents in India closely match national data on public trust in science. In a survey across 68 countries published last year, India was the country with the second-highest trust in scientists after Egypt. Mede, who was one of the study’s authors, thinks that strong pro-science rhetoric from the Indian government could play a part in the country’s high trust levels.

The Indian constitution even lists developing a “scientific temper” — meaning one that is led by logic and evidence instead of belief or superstition — among the duties of its citizens. Mede says that Indian scientists might view this pro-science political climate as a proxy for public trust.

Nature’s survey data for Japan suggests that scientists there feel that public trust is relatively stable, even if the actual level of trust might be modest, says Sotaro Shibayama, an economist of science at the University of Tokyo. This makes sense to him, because he thinks that science is less politicized in his country than it is in nations where a higher proportion felt trust had dropped. Studies indicate that trust in science fluctuates in Japan as well, Shibayama says, “but these fluctuations may be smaller than in countries where science has become more closely entangled with political and ideological divisions”.

When asked what is driving the falling levels of trust, the responses indicate that scientists view distrust more as a problem originating externally, rather than something caused from within. Some 69% said that misinformation was the main cause, followed by political pressure or influence on science (62%) and a lack of public understanding of science (54%). Survey-takers could select more than one driver and this question was asked only of those who answered that trust had declined.

Only 24% thought that increased scrutiny and scepticism of experts was a main driver of falling trust and just 23% thought that scientists’ communication with the public was to blame. “We often do not have training in science communication, nor do we really need it,” wrote one early-career Earth and atmospheric scientist in Portugal. “We are paid, and should be paid, to do science.”

Have people stopped trusting science? The data tell a surprising story

Have people stopped trusting science? The data tell a surprising story

But Mede says that the evidence that misinformation and a lack of public understanding erode trust significantly is “much thinner and more mixed than one would expect”. Shared values and transparency might matter more. A UK study published in September found that trust was shaped less by whether the public viewed scientists as experts and more by whether scientists were ‘on their side’. Perceptions of openness and transparency also mattered for trust, the study found: 73% of those with high trust in scientists agreed that scientists were generally open and transparent, compared with just 10% of those with low trust.

Misconduct and scientific fraud were not included among the reasons Nature’s survey-takers could select as drivers of falling public trust — an omission of the survey design, in hindsight. But in free-text answers, some respondents said that they felt scientists were partly to blame for public opinion turning against them. One social scientist in the United States wrote that “rampant fraud” in research, such as fabricated data and scientists racing to publish as much as possible with scant thought to the value of their research, has rightly drained public trust. He says that he feels “furious” that academics have undermined their own credibility. “I literally am embarrassed to tell people in my community what I do for a living,” he writes.

Another US respondent, an engineering researcher who said he comes from a cattle ranching family in Texas, wrote that academia “has earned every bit of scepticism that it receives from the public”. Most scientists don’t understand working-class people, he wrote. “When we use the degrees we earned at protected bubbles on university campuses to say that ‘we know best, give us power’, we have to accept that we are nearly always wrong.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it comes to English football’s best atmospheres, few can match the noise and fury of a packed Elland Road.

Since joining Leeds United from Yorkshire rivals Sheffield United in 2024, Jayden Bogle has been able to experience this on a regular basis, with his defensive efforts and lung-busting runs forward bringing the cheers of the Elland Road faithful week-in, week-out.

This backing helped Bogle’s side win promotion back to the Premier League in the right-back’s first season in West Yorkshire, which was followed up by a respectable 14th-place finish back in the top flight last term.

Leeds’ return to the Premier League last season came against Everton, a match which left a lasting impression on Bogle.

“The first game of last season [a 1-0 win over Everton] was top, that atmosphere,” he tells FourFourTwo.

“You really feel the impact of what the fans and the stadium can do, especially when we're making chances or someone puts in a big tackle or block. You can feel the energy instantly from the fans.”

The Leeds fanbase has taken its fair share of knocks over the years, and while Bogle knows just how important building this authentic connection with the fans is, it has to be done in the right way.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“As players, you work all year round to stay as professional as you can,” he continues. “You try to have that relationship with the fans, but you've got to stay professional at the same time.”

Leeds’ promotion campaign, which saw them win the Championship title with virtually the last kick of the season, sparked huge celebrations in the city, climaxing in an estimated 150,000 fans lining the streets for an open top bus parade.

For Bogle, this was finally a chance to share in the moment with the club’s supporters.

"On that day, it was nice to be able to really bond with them, especially after the parade.

“Everyone was on the same page, happy and enjoying it. When we got on the bus and headed towards the city centre, it was something I'd never seen before – flares going off, people everywhere.

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#808. Hosting World Cup means decade of excitement - Weir

Caroline Weir says it is "amazing" that Scotland will host the World Cup finals

Scotland captain Caroline Weir says hosting the 2035 Women's World Cup along with England, Northern Ireland and Wales will usher in "an amazing decade of excitement" for the game in her homeland.

World governing body Fifa confirmed on Monday that the United Kingdom will host a football World Cup for the first time since England won the men's tournament on home soil in 1966.

Scotland's national stadium at Hampden Park in Glasgow and Hibernian's Easter Road Stadium in Leith are among 19 venues chosen for the 39-day competition involving 48 teams.

At the age of 31 now, Weir would have to show unusual longevity to still be playing at that point, but she still considers it "amazing news, not just for young players that hope to play there but for us, in this period in between, to develop the women's game in Scotland - and to push it.

"So I think it's amazing news and I think it's going to be an amazing decade of excitement leading into this World Cup".

Andreatta's masterplan to shock Sweden & take Scots to World Cup

Big wins as Celtic, Rangers, City & Hearts progress

The Lyon midfielder has already played for Scotland the only time they have so far qualified for a World Cup finals - in 2019.

"As a young, aspiring footballer watching football on TV growing up, for your home country to actually host a tournament itself, and the World Cup itself, the biggest tournament in football, is the most amazing thing," Weir said.

"So, if I was a 10 or 11 year old girl now, I would be thinking this is the best news ever and I'm going to work and practice and hope that, one day, I am representing Scotland in a home nations tournament playing at Hampden Park in a World Cup for Scotland.

"I don't think it gets any bigger or better than that."

Angie Hind, Scotland Under-23 head coach and Scottish FA player pathway manager, also thinks it will prove inspirational to the young players under her charge.

"If you think of the young players who are involved in our pathway right now, from 13 years old right through the 23s that I take, that's the future," the former Scotland midfielder told BBC Scotland.

"That's very much those players who will be pulling on a Scotland jersey when we are part of that World Cup."

Hind pointed out that it "fits perfectly" with Project 2035, announced this month by SFA and Scottish government, designed to boost the long-term growth of the girls and women's game.

For SFA head of women's and girls football Shirley Martin, it is a "tremendous milestone" considering holding a World Cup had been such "a game changer" for previous hosts.

"Ten years ago, a home World Cup have felt like a dream and now it's happening," she told BBC Radio 5 live. "I think it shows how far women's football has come."

Martin pointed out that the SFA hopes to "double our participation over that time" as well as improving coaching, referees, clubs and facilities - and are already doing so.

However, she admitted: "The one thing we need to do is increase the crowds that come to matches."

#807. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, he comes up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posts them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

This information is a guide and is constantly changing. Please check the National Careers Service website for the latest information and all the qualifications needed and the GOV.UK website for more on T-levels.

For careers advice in all parts of the UK visit: National Careers Service (England), nidirect (Northern Ireland), My World of Work (Scotland) and Careers Wales (Wales).

Bruno Guimaraes’ return to St James’ Park in Arsenal colours was meant to rub salt into the wounds of Newcastle’s summer exodus, but it galvanised the Magpies who channeled the emotion into a second-half comeback.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It was, for many, the moment Newcastle United ceased to be a force in English football. Bruno Guimaraes’ move to Arsenal was traumatic, and from the club are yet to fully recover.

He was the best player, the talisman, the captain and the one big hope. Without him, an entirely new identity needs to be forged. But Newcastle, and new manager Matthias Jaissle have floundered ever since they parted ways.

Arsenal’s trip north was always going to be about one man. Guimaraes hasn’t been universally derided by Newcastle fans in the way Alexander Isak was, and was made clear by a low key, if still frosty reception when he stepped off the team bus. It was more pantomime than persona non grata.

His exit arguably cut deeper than Isak’s, and those of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali earlier in the summer, but has polarised the fanbase.

For some, his service in leading Newcastle to their first domestic trophy cements his legacy regardless of how ill-timed and controversial his departure was. With so much change at the club going on around him, compounded by the resignation of Eddie Howe in late July, it became clear Guimaraes’ ambitions would no longer be realised on Tyneside.

Seeing Isak, Tonali and Gordon leave with a chance of winning trophies, doubling their wages or both will have stung for the Brazilian. When he arrived in January 2022, he genuinely believed Newcastle would be able to win the Champions League.

Suddenly, they were proudly and publicly embracing a trading model in the transfer market, ripping up their previous approach and starting again. Guimaraes was still central to their plans, but at 28 years of age (now 29), he could no longer wait for phase two of the Newcastle project, especially when promises from phase one remained unfulfilled.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

But over the last four years, he went above and beyond other imports when it came to building a relationship with supporters, talking openly about being an adopted Geordie and wanting to emulate Alan Shearer in becoming a lasting hero.

It was that strength of feeling which Newcastle hoped would coax him into staying another season and led to supporters truly believing in loyalty. But in their time of need, the captain abandoned ship. He was well within his rights to depart, and it is hard to criticise given Arsenal already look like Premier League champions elect.

Yet, having talked up his love for life at Newcastle in the build up, reaffirming how difficult it was to leave, he couldn’t have complained when he was cast in the role of villain.

If his afternoon was summed up in one moment, though, it was his former midfield protege at Newcastle, tapping him on the back as Harvey Barnes swept home a second half equaliser.

Malick Thiaw went on to put the home side in front, only for Noni Madueke to restore parity once again. It was a slow burn, but ultimately, Guimaraes’ presence united Newcastle on the pitch and in the stands.

The expectation was it would be instant and Arsenal would be under siege from a black and white storm whipped up by anger in his direction. Instead, in the first half, it was tame, and when Eberechi Eze opened the scoring, it felt like game over already.

There have been reports in recent weeks suggesting the players do not understand Jaissle’s methods. It certainly felt like that at times; Lukas Hornicek, required to confidently play out from the back, looked shaken every time he had the ball at his feet.

Joe Willock was seen asking questions on his role more than once; Jaissle looked on full of exasperation but, it seemed, with very few answers. A third meek home defeat in succession seemed a formality. Once the game restarted, though, everything shifted.

Jaissle, to his credit, made bold choices, bringing off the one bright spark in the first half, Sean Steur and replacing him with Jacob Ramsey. Tino Livramento and Anthony Elanga were also introduced and Newcastle came alive.

The power, the drive and the ferocity of St James’ Park spurred them on. Suddenly, Jaissle’s approach seemed clear; there was something tangible to build from, a blueprint.

“Everything started with the press,” Thiaw said after the game. “If you win the ball high and early, there is space to attack vertically and directly. It is about how you work off the ball.

“The manager kept it really calm at half time, he knew what we had to do and made good changes. When you are a squad, everybody has to be ready. We used [the crowd’s reaction to Guimaraes] as fuel and we felt that on the pitch.”

Thiaw is one of the players who has stepped into what Jaissle called a “leadership vacuum” in the squad after Guimaraes left. He insists the squad is still backing their manager.

“There are always noises in football, especially outside of the locker room,” he added. “We know what we have to do and what we have to deliver. We are giving everything for the club and the manager.

“If we don’t believe, who will? We will keep improving and we need them. We are all in this together.”

Starting with Arsenal, there is a run of four very tough and potentially season-defining games for Jaissle and Newcastle. Brighton follows, before two home games in a week against Manchester United and Sunderland. It is still far from perfect, but green shoots of optimism may just be emerging.

#805. German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?

The German economy is growing again, albeit slightly. However, economists warn that without reforms, higher productivity and solid public finances, a loss of prosperity and growing debt threaten future generations.

Is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.

At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I said here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.

The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.

Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.

"[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.

Merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz said in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.

Given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz said when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.

The economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.

"The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," said Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending."

The chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that."

But these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.

At the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.

"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she said.

The government is currently in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in new debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.

The economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.

Germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," said Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.

The so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, said the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.

"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer said.

According to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an issue in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz said there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially when it comes to social security systems.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a company can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.

According to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.

If the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it said in the report. "New technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop."

But innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.

New evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.

There continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.

The intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a new study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association showed that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.

This article was originally written in German.
