#771. Carra: Chelsea must sign centre-back or achieve nothing

Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher analysed Chelsea's leaky defence on Monday Night Football, highlighting the partnership of Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana as a major concern; watch Nott'm Forest vs Chelsea on Friday, live on Sky Sports; kick-off 8pm

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jamie Carragher believes Chelsea must sign a dominant centre-back or they will have "no chance of achieving anything".

Chelsea have conceded 20 goals in 11 Premier League games this season and were thrashed 4-1 at home to Leeds on Saturday, which has put pressure on new manager Xabi Alonso, with his side sitting eighth and already 12 points behind leaders Arsenal.

Leeds overpowered Chelsea with their physicality, as Dominic Calvert-Lewin bullied centre-backs Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana, exposing their weak defence the same way Sunderland's Brian Brobbey did in their 1-0 win before the international break.

Chelsea are five points behind fourth-placed Liverpool and are already without European football this season - but Carragher feels qualifying for the Champions League will be a difficult task with their current centre-back pairing.

"Chelsea have got a massive problem at centre-back and if they don't change it in January, they're going to have a big problem in terms of where they feel they should be this season with the Champions League," he said on Monday Night Football.

"Colwill at Sunderland against Brobbey gave the penalty away, and the manager took him off at half-time. Fofana's performance against Man United, especially in the first half, was one of the worst you'll see from a centre-back this season.

"As a partnership, this will never work because they're not physical enough and there's no real leader there.

"It almost feels like you've got two novices playing, but one cost £75m, and Colwill has been talked up a lot not just at Chelsea but at international level as well."

Chelsea signed centre-back Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace for £51m in the summer, but he has missed the last three matches with a hamstring injury.

"Those two (Colwill and Fofana) can't play in a back four as a two, but it reminds me of myself at Liverpool," said Carragher. "We didn't fix it defensively and we were seen as weak, conceding from set pieces and long throws. It wasn't until we signed Sami Hyypia, 6ft 4in, dominant centre-back, leader, great player, that it changed for us.

"This is not going to change with what they have. Lacroix is a decent player, that's a sticking plaster until the next transfer window in January or the end of the season. Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they've got absolutely no chance of achieving anything."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Chelsea have kept the fourth fewest clean sheets in Europe this calendar year, which largely predates Alonso's tenure, although Carragher has been surprised by the former Bayer Leverkusen and Real Madrid head coach's style.

"There's a lot of talk now about Xabi Alonso and I think watching Chelsea this season, they haven't been that impressive even when they've won games in terms of how I think we all felt they would play," he added.

"Everybody had this idea, myself included, who had watched Leverkusen play, you think of the player Xabi Alonso would play, the Spanish influence and managed by Pep Guardiola. You're expecting Chelsea to be more of a possession-based team and when you watch them the football isn't amazing and they rely on the front three a lot.

"Cole Palmer has dropped off in the last few weeks and Joao Pedro has been injured as well. When they've all been there, it always felt like there was an overreliance on that front three. The goal on the weekend was a direct play; you can get goals in different ways, but there hasn't been that intricate football that we were expecting."

In his latest Sky Sports column, Paul Merson has raised doubts about whether Alonso is good enough as Chelsea manager after Saturday's home loss to Leeds.

Merson believes Liverpool may have snubbed Alonso for the head coach role - eventually taken by Andoni Iraola - due to concerns about his pedigree.

He told Sky Sports: "My biggest worry is that Liverpool could have had Xabi Alonso and they chose not to. Obviously, Liverpool didn't think he was good enough.

"Alonso took the Chelsea job, and Liverpool sacked Arne Slot two weeks later. You can't tell me that Liverpool couldn't have spoken to Alonso and say: 'Don't take the Chelsea job, we're going to take you'.

"He was out of a job as well, Liverpool could have had him and he'd have gone there all day long. So why didn't they take him? Did they know something that we're seeing now?

"It just always sits in my mind. That was my worry - and now it's playing out.

"If this was Liam Rosenior in charge at Chelsea and getting these results, he'd be in major trouble. One hundred per cent, he'd be in trouble. And remember, Rosenior didn't have Morgan Rogers in his Chelsea team, bought for £116m.

"But it's because of the unbelievable job he did at Bayer Leverkusen that everybody is thinking: it will be alright."

#770. Argentina midfielder Paredes collapses during TV interview

Leandro Paredes played for PSG, Roma and Juventus during his time in Europe

World Cup winning midfielder Leandro Paredes collapsed while giving a post-match interview minutes after winning a trophy with Boca Juniors.

The former Paris St-Germain midfielder, 32, was suffering with the heat and humidity in Barranquilla, Colombia, where Boca won the Copa Sudamericana by beating Atletico Mineiro of Brazil 2-0.

He was replaced during the second half, then collapsed while being interviewed on television, with pictures showing a journalist trying to break his fall.

After some treatment Argentine Paredes was able to walk to the dressing room and joined in with his team's celebrations.

"Thanks to everyone for the messages, it was just dizziness," he said on Instagram, external after the match.

Heat was a discussion before the game with forecasts predicting tempertures could reach 32C and humidity around 80%.

Boca manager Rodolfo Arruabarrena said he noticed the midfielder's difficulties during the second half.

"He felt dizzy towards the end of the first half," Arruabarrena said.

"He improved a little during the break, but after 10 minutes in the second half you could see he was struggling."

Paredes started his career with Boca before moving to Europe in 2015.

The victory for Boca ended an 18-year international trophy drought for the Argentine side.

By securing their 19th international cup, Boca also became South America's most decorated club since 1960, overtaking domestic rivals Independiente who have 18.

#769. Frick delivers on 'heavy metal football' promise

Mario Frick joined Aberdeen after leaving Luzern

If "heavy metal football" is what Aberdeen did, indeed, serve up at Kilmarnock on Saturday, Dons supporters will be eager to see more of this type of concert.

New head coach Mario Frick used the phrase in the build-up to his first game in charge and his team did not disappoint.

The 4-2 Rugby Park victory was bombastic, chaotic and end-to-end - just one of six goal-laden Scottish Premiership games on Saturday.

The four Aberdeen strikes - two from Kevin Nisbet and one each from Brad Lyons and Findlay Marshall - showed Aberdeen's attackers at their best with fine finishing.

In the work in progress column, though, is defending, with the visitors lapsing badly for Killie goals scored by Greg Kiltie and Tyreece John-Jules.

All in all, it was an ideal start for former Luzern boss Frick.

Aberdeen's Frick starts with win in six-goal thriller at Kilmarnock

Watch new Aberdeen boss Frick score against Scotland

Frick was not a complete unknown to Scottish football when he was appointed during the international break - but the reference point was somewhat obscure.

Playing for Liechtenstein at Hampden in 2010, Frick gave the visitors a shock second-half lead.

The end of that game was reminiscent of the kind of heavy metal the head coach was talking about pre-match as Stephen McManus headed Scotland's winner after Kenny Miller's leveller.

Speaking after his Premiership bow, the former Luzern boss described himself as "very happy, very proud" of his new team.

"With only three training session, you can see so many attacking patterns in that first half, which was amazing," he told BBC Scotland.

"We struggled the first few minutes with some players that hadn't played in a long long time and the 1-0 lead helped. First half was very good, the second half, complicated, because Kilmarnock played very well. We were very lucky, but at the end, I think it is a deserved victory and we are very happy."

When asked if he was happy with the players trying to show his style, Frick replied: "Yes, for sure, after two training sessions, I saw a lot of it in the first half.

"It is a good start for us, but it is just the beginning."

Former Scotland midfielder Derek Ferguson took in the match at Rugby Park and was impressed with the visitors.

"As an attacking force, I thought they were good to watch," the former Rangers player said.

"They've got a big game on Tuesday night, against Rangers, so Rangers will need to be at their best, on their toes if they're going to get a result.

"It was the perfect result, obviously, for the manager coming in.

"There was more energy, more legs, more running power. They were winning a lot of the duels.

"It's something to build on, but they've got to work on that defence. They've got to be more solid if they're going to go forward."

Next up Ibrox and a season's third meeting with Rangers.

The two previous encounters, in the Premiership and League Cup semi-final, finished 1-0 to the Ibrox side, with the winning goal coming in the second half both times.

Meetings of Aberdeen and Rangers are typically just as fraught as the Rugby Park game on Saturday.

So, more heavy metal? It probably won't be smooth jazz.

We asked for your views following Aberdeen's 4-2 win over Kilmarnock.

Allan: One simple question. Why was [Ante] Palaversa nowhere to be seen under Stephen Robinson? I think the fans are due an explanation as to why both he and [Nicky] Devlin fell so far down the pecking order.

Brian: Much, much better is probably an understatement. Great entertainment and a big threat going forward and,as long as we score one more (at least) than the opposition then I will be happy. It is very noticeable that Jack Milne is much more steady when Nicky Devlin is playing. I am looking forward to the rest of this campaign.

Mike: Green shoots of recovery evident. Working as a unit from back to front has been a rarity at Aberdeen. If this is only after three training sessions, I am drooling at the mouth for what's to come. Stiff test on Tuesday, but the confidence must be there so nothing to fear.

Fred: Very positive start under the new manager. Good to see some direct attacking play but still a problem defending. An acid test coming against Rangers.

#768. Yoro sees red as Ngumoha shines - Liverpool v Man Utd player ratings

Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man Utd

Mauricio Pochettino's reign as Manchester United manager got off to a dismal start as his side were beaten 4-0 by rivals Liverpool after playing 82 minutes with 10 men.

Here's how BBC Sport rated the players - and you can see how you scored them below.

Alisson Becker: Caught one cross and took a few goal-kicks. Made a good save to deny Bruno Fernandes in stoppage time. Had little else to do. 6

Ronald Araujo: Never really tested defensively. Made a few contributions going forward. 7

Jeremy Jacquet: Went shoulder to shoulder with Bryan Mbeumo in the box at 0-0, although a penalty against the French defender would have been harsh. 6

Virgil van Dijk: Organised the defence well. Also had a header well-saved at 0-0 and nodded another wide in the second half. 7

Milos Kerkez: Always keen to drive Liverpool up the pitch. Had some nice link-ups with Rio Ngumoha. 7

Dominik Szoboszlai: Fantastic driven free-kick to open the scoring. Went close a few more times with long shots and generally bossed the midfield. 8

Alexis Mac Allister: Did all the simple things right and allowed others to shine around him. Forced Senne Lammens into a top save in the first half. 7

Bradley Barcola: Missed a few chances to score his first league goal for Liverpool when through one-vs-one. Showed his electric pace to set up his side's third. 7

Florian Wirtz: Readjusted well to net Liverpool's second and assisted their fourth. Five goals in four games for club and country now and looks close to his creative best. 8

Rio Ngumoha: So direct and skilful. Scored Liverpool's third with a calm finish. Also set up their second after easily beating Diogo Dalot. Club and country have a real talent on their hands. 9

Alexander Isak: Led the line well but missed some big chances. Won the free-kick that resulted in Szoboszlai's goal and led to Leny Yoro's sending off. 6

Victor Munoz (on 72, Barcola): Good cameo and took his goal well, curling it into the far corner. 7

Trey Nyoni (on 72, Mac Allister): Looked bright. Had a shot go just over. 6

Subs not used: Chiesa, Mamardashvili, McConell, Tsimikas.

Senne Lammens: Could he have done better with the opener? Good save to deny Mac Allister and some decent stops after that. 6

Leny Yoro: Did he have to make the tackle on Isak? It was almost as though he thought about whether he should and decided the answer was yes. Given Liverpool scored from the free-kick it was a bad decision. 4

Matthijs de Ligt: First Premier League start in almost 12 months in middle of a back three turned into a nightmare with the early error that led to opening goal and Yoro red card. Struggled from that moment on. 4

Lisandro Martinez: Fully extended by Liverpool's attack. The least bad of the visitors' starting defence, but that isn't saying much. Exposed completely by Barcola for Liverpool's third. 5

Diogo Dalot: Given a torrid time by Ngumoha, which prompted Pochettino to bring on Maguire. Tries hard but it's not enough. 5

Youri Tielemans: Concerns about a midfield partnership with Mainoo emerge again. Not having the sustained impact required for a player of his experience. 4

Kobbie Mainoo: Twenty-one-year-old being asked to shoulder so much responsibility in an ailing team. New midfield recruits have not helped him. 5

Bryan Mbeumo: Couple of decent bursts came to nothing, then sacrificed after Yoro red card. Received consoling pat on the head from his new boss. 5

Bruno Fernandes: Early free-kick just wide and shot straight at Alisson. Given the carnage at Old Trafford this season, no wonder contract talks on hold. Furious at free-kick given against him when he thought he was through. 5

Patrick Dorgu: Asked to do an awful lot, initially as wing-back, then further back. Lucky Barcola fluffed his lines or his failure to keep an offside line would have been exposed. 5

Matheus Cunha: Tried to keep simmering frustration in check. Not easy in a losing side with no service. Replaced at the break. 5

Harry Maguire (on 22, Mbeumo): Couldn't have expected to be called on so soon. Went into middle of back three and immediately blocked an Isak effort to prevent a third goal. Tried hard. 5

Joshua Zirkzee (on 46, Cunha): Pre-match rumours of a rare start proved unfounded. Replaced Cunha at half-time and asked to bring a different skillset to the number nine role. More physical but not as good and lost possession too easily. 4

Mason Mount (on 65, Tielemans): Only on for a couple of minutes when attempted crossfield pass went to Liverpool player and eventually a third goal. 5

Noussair Mazraoui (on 65, Dorgu): Not really sure what he was supposed to do. Tried to push forward as United's poor control brought more pressure. 4

Subs not used: Heaton, Amad Diallo, Heaven, Lacey.

#767. Metcalf denies poking DeJean in the eyes as NFL rules out suspension

DK Metcalf was ejected from the Pittsburgh Steelers' 19-16 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles after appearing to reach into Cooper DeJean's facemask and poke him in the eyes; the NFL will not suspend the receiver but he could be fined, according to sources

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Pittsburgh Steelers wide receiver DK Metcalf will not be suspended by the NFL for appearing to poke Philadelphia Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean in the eyes but he could still be fined, according to sources.

Metcalf denied that he intentionally stuck his fingers in the Eagles defender's facemask when addressing the media on Monday.

Having been ejected from a game for the third time in his career during the second half of the Steelers' 19-16 loss on Sunday, Metcalf initially said that he "couldn't remember" the incident, before backtracking and saying that he was trying to send a message to DeJean to "stop pushing me".

Metcalf had caught only one pass for two yards before being sent to the locker room after being flagged twice for personal fouls following a couple of confrontations with DeJean.

The NFL will review Metcalf's actions during the game for potential fines as part of its standard disciplinary review process, ESPN and NFL Network reported, but he escapes a suspension.

The 28-year-old was banned for two games last season for swiping at a fan in Detroit and was shown the door twice earlier in his career while playing for the Seattle Seahawks.

Asked why this keeps happening, Metcalf told reporters: "I think you got to ask the people that seem to do that to me".

Metcalf noted that opponents trying to get under his skin is nothing new, saying that San Francisco 49ers players attempted to do that regularly during the Seahawks' frequent meetings with their NFC West rivals.

The two-time Pro Bowler, who is on pace for career lows in receptions and yards receiving this season, declined to blame the heated interaction on frustration, pointing out that the Steelers are "winning", though Pittsburgh (6-4) has dropped two straight after losing in Philadelphia.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Steelers coach Mike McCarthy called Metcalf's actions "unacceptable" but said he needed more information before deciding whether to take any action.

Metcalf did not appear to be worried about being disciplined by the Steelers or the NFL. "You've got to ask [Pittsburgh general manager] Omar [Khan] that, or anybody else other than DeKaylin," Metcalf said, using his given name.

The highest-paid wide receiver in team history also added that the Steelers need to "score points when we get the ball and not stall on third down or get a turnover on downs, stay on the field so our defense can stay off the field".

Pittsburgh remain firmly in playoff position as Thanksgiving looms but face a daunting stretch over the next three weeks that includes a pair of meeting with first-placed teams in their division - the Denver Broncos (8-2) and Jacksonville Jaguars (7-3), as well as a key clash with fellow AFC wildcard contenders the Houston Texans (4-6).

#766. Holders Celtic win 17-0 in Women's Scottish Cup

Isabella Fisher scored four goals in Celtic's win

Holders Celtic breezed through to the fourth round of the Women's Scottish Cup with a 17-0 victory over Forfar Farmington.

Morgan Cross and Casey Howe both netted hat-tricks, Isabella Fisher scored four times and Amy Gallacher bagged a double.

Lauren Doran-Barr, Addie Handley, Maria McAneny and Evie Rabjohn also scored and Forfar conceded an own goal.

Last season's beaten finalists, Rangers, were 5-0 victors at home to Motherwell.

Mijke Roelfsema opened the scoring with her first Rangers goal, Eilidh Austin made it two and Laura Berry converted a penalty shortly before going off injured.

Fallon Connolly-Jackson got her maiden Rangers goal early in the second half and Hannah Blake completed the scoring.

Glasgow City defeated Cambusdoon 10-0. Leah Lane scored her first City goal, with Kelly Brady, Lisa Forrest, Abi Harrison, Yuuka Kurosaki, Jesi Rossman and Emily Whelan also on target.

Sofia Maatta netted twice and Cambusdoon conceded an own goal.

Reigning Scottish champions Heart of Midlothian won 6-0 away to Stenhousemuir.

Lucy Jane Hope put the visitors in front and Jenny Smith doubled their lead. Ava Crawford got the third, Monica Forsyth also netted and Hope and Forsyth added to the tally.

Montrose won 13-0 at Dunipace, with Neve Guthrie, Kaela McDonald-Nguah and Hannah Stewart each scoring once, Francesca Ogilvie netting twice, Darcie Miller bagging a hat-trick and Demi Taylor picking up a four-goal haul, with an own goal also aiding the visitors.

Spartans were 11-2 winners at home to Bonnyrigg Rose. Zara Andrews and Ronaigh Douglas both scored once, there were doubles for Emily Cadell, Tegan Reynolds and Izzy Young, while Emma McMurdo scored a hat-trick.

Mya Christie, Holly Daniel, Christie again and Briana Salvetti all netted in Aberdeen's 4-0 home win over Dryburgh Athletic.

SWPL2 side Boroughmuir Thistle won 2-1 on penalties against top-flight Partick Thistle after a 1-1 draw. Imogen Longcake gave the visitors a second-half lead, but Amy Denholm levelled to force extra time.

Falkirk were 7-0 winners at home to Renfrew. Maisy Stewart, Skye Neillie, Mhari Smith, Caitlin McFarlane and Olivia Murphy all scored first-half goals, with McFarlane and Emma Lawson adding to the rout after the break.

Queen's Park beat Dundee United 2-1, with Ellie Kane and Darcy Molloy putting the hosts two up at the break and Lucy Stevenson replying in the second half.

Rossvale won 3-2 at home to Gartcairn. Maddie Wilson and Sarah Petherick had Rossvale 2-0 up, but Clare Docherty replied for the visitors before the break. Petherick's second proved to be the winner, with Gartcairn's Madison Maxwell netting a late consolation.

Livingston v Hamilton Academical was abandoned at half-time with Hamilton a goal up, while Inverurie Loco Works v Bishopton, Kilmarnock v Hibernian and Westdyke v St Johnstone were postponed.

#764. Legendary Jewelry Designer Paolo Bulgari Dead at 89

Paolo Bulgari—whose Bvlgari Group created unforgettable jewelry designs for stars like Elizabeth Taylor and Zendaya—has died at age 89.

Paolo Bulgari—famed jewelry designer and chairman of the Bvlgari Group—has died, the company confirmed on social media Nov. 21. He was 89.

“It is with deep sadness that we learned of the passing of Paolo Bulgari, grandson of the company’s founder Sotirio Bulgari and Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984,” the company said in a statement shared to Instagram. “Our deepest condolences go to his family, friends and all those who had the honor of sharing this journey with him.”

“Thank you, Mr. Paolo,” they added, “your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come.”

Born in Rome, Italy, in 1937, Bulgari—who shared four kids with ex-wife Alice Valli as well as two kids with wife Maite Caprio—was destined to carry on the family business from a young age.

“Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960,” the statement explained, “specializing in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world’s leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style.”

And it wasn’t long until he started making his own mark on the brand.

“A true creative soul, he poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers,” added the statement, “leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewelry.”

In fact, Bulgari, alongside his brothers Gianni Bulgari and Nicola Bulgari, played an integral role in shaping the brand’s distinctive style, becoming known for their use of bold shapes and standout gems.

They also expanded the business from jewelry into watches, perfumes and even hotels.

And over the decades, the brand’s creations have adorned stars from Elizabeth Taylor and Princess Diana to Zendaya and Anne Hathaway.

Just last month, Kim Kardashian said she might just “faint” in a video shared to Instagram Oct. 28 while getting a private tour of Taylor’s jewelry collection at the Bvlgari store in Italy, in which she was able to try on one of the late actress’ beloved pieces—an emerald and diamond necklace gifted to her by Richard Burton in 1962.

As Kardashian put it, “I am freaking out!”

And she of course had to thank her stylist Law Roach for making the dream come true, calling him on the phone to thank him for the “best” birthday present ever.

And while it’s true that Bulgari’s influence on fashion has stood the test of time, that’s because he believed “everything can be a source of inspiration.”

As he used to say, per Bvlgari’s statement, “There are no rules in creativity. Never.”

#763. Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.

"Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he said on Sunday.

But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.

"There are people who truly care about the future of football, people who aren't driven by financial interests," Klopp said ahead of Germany's Nations League match against the Netherlands on Monday.

"If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement."

If that person is waiting in the wings, they're leaving it late to step on the stage. Despite a raft of federations and continental confederations, including Germany, UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia), calling for Infantino's head in the wake of his plan to sell off part of the World Cup earlier this year, the incumbent appears to have stopped the bleeding.

That plan, which involved forming a subsidiary arm of FIFA called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors including Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner — was widely panned before being abandoned.

It followed on from widespread criticism of Infantino's awarding of a new FIFA Peace Prize to Trump, the overturning of a red card for US national team player Folarin Balogun, and with Trump's involvement, at the World Cup and a host of other controversies.

Since then, though, many public critics have backtracked amid FIFA promising to release an extra $2.7bn (€2.45bn) from its reserves over the next four years to the federations, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn.

Perhaps the most significant of these u-turns came from the AFC, who went from saying Infantino had committed a "fundamental breach of trust" in August, to offering the Swiss its "full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president" in October.

Those words were spoken by AFC President, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who ran against Infantino when he first won the top job at FIFA in 2016. He will not run again and said that "my feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," in regard to Infantino.

Proof that the sentiment is not universal comes in the shape of Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA). Tashima is one of only two people to confirm they will oppose Infantino in the March 2027 presidential elections.

The 68-year-old is a well respected figure in Asian football politics and will have no problem meeting the threshold of support from five of FIFA's 211 federations. This is not like the other candidate, former Swiss international player Ramon Vega, who is an enormous outsider. Tashima appears to be running on the basis that he will be able to chart a calmer path at FIFA.

"I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association," Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. "It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world."

But the numbers are against him. Though support from within the confederations may not be total, the backing of AFC and the African confederation (CAF) is a huge boost for Infantino, with those two alone making up 101 votes, almost enough for a majority.

In fact, the only real concern remaining for Infantino remains UEFA. The European federation, headed by Aleksander Ceferin, is a major revenue source for FIFA but the two organizations are at loggerheads. As well as a war of words, UEFA are seeking to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against Infantino in regards to FFE. FIFA have called this a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition".

But, so far, UEFA has not put up a candidate. Former Arsenal coach turned FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger was thought to be a contender but has now ruled himself out. Wenger's compatriot, Philippe Diallo, has since emerged as another option, with The Guardian reporting on Monday that the French Football Federation president could be announced on Tuesday.

While Europe is football's powerbase, particularly from a club perspective, UEFA will need Diallo, or any candidate they can convince to run, to win votes from outside its 55 nations to have any chance of success, particularly with Tashima likely to split any challenge. Even if a candidate appears before the November 18 deadline, Klopp's hope for change appears to be a long shot.

#760. Has Verstappen feud reignited at wrong time for Russell?

The feud between George Russell and Max Verstappen reignited in spectacular style in Las Vegas following a clash between the pair in practice; watch the Qatar Grand Prix live on Sky Sports this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The reignition of the long-running feud between George Russell and Max Verstappen has added an entertaining twist to the end of the 2026 Formula 1 season, but it may not be what the Mercedes driver needed at this moment.

Russell and Verstappen clashed during final practice at the Las Vegas Grand Prix when the Red Bull driver, slightly cheekily, snatched track position from his Mercedes rival as they both prepared for push laps.

Irked by Verstappen's actions, which he later said he felt breached a gentleman's agreement the drivers share, Russell attempted to reclaim track position from the weaving Red Bull, with the pair making slight contact.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The stewards summoned the two drivers following the session as they conducted an investigation, before handing Verstappen a warning.

The incident came less than a month on from Verstappen being involved a similar incident with Racing Bulls driver Liam Lawson during practice at the Mexico City Grand Prix, which resulted in both drivers being given one-place grid penalties.

Speaking to Sky Italy later that evening, Russell said: "There's nothing in the rules to say you cannot overtake someone who is starting a lap but when you do this, you are screwing this person over and he does this week in, week out with many drivers and everybody accepts it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody's got to stand up to that guy."

F1: What is going on at Ferrari? - 'They are learning NOTHING!'

Max Verstappen victorious in Vegas and questions for Ferrari after collision - The Verdict

Magic in Vegas! Dynamo stuns crew on race day!

Las Vegas GP: NEW ANGLES! Lewis Hamilton spins after contact with Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc

F1 team-mate 2026 head-to-head: Qualifying, Race, Sprint latest scores, results from Formula 1 season

Russell's comments came after the result of qualifying in Las Vegas dictated that the pair would start together on the front row, with Verstappen ahead in pole position.

That setup a Saturday night showdown, in which the pair engaged in a thrilling battle for the lead for much of the race, before Russell dropped behind Kimi Antonelli in the latter stages and then drove into a barrier attempting to pass his Mercedes team-mate.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Verstappen reacted on team radio with apparent glee having seen Russell's error in his mirrors, and then, after closing out a superb victory, further stuck the boot into the British driver during the post-race press conference for the top three.

The four-time world champion said: "The thing is, he speaks a lot next to the track. And honestly, for me, it doesn't really bother me because he's so far below my level that it doesn't really make any sense for me anyway to try and challenge that. So, it doesn't bother me.

"And today, karma is a b****. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening [when Russell crashed]. I was like, 'fantastic, my day is only getting better.' And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

With less than five months separating them in age, Russell and Verstappen have been racing each other in karting since they were children.

While Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff reflected in Las Vegas that the feud may have stretched back to those days, the first notable F1 flashpoint between the pair came in the 2023 Azerbaijan Sprint when they made contact through several corners on the opening lap.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

In a post-race exchange broadcast to the world, Verstappen barked at Russell to "expect next time the same" and swore at the Mercedes driver as he walked away. He would later refer to Russell as "princess George" in an interview with the Dutch media.

A spectacular fall out between the pair then occurred towards the end of the 2024 season, after Verstappen felt Russell had played an unreasonably key role in the Red Bull driver being given a grid penalty that cost him pole for the Qatar Grand Prix.

Verstappen said in Qatar that he had "lost all respect" for Russell, who then responded with a remarkable explosive verbal attack on the Dutchman the following week at the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Russell said Verstappen had threatened to put him "in the wall" in Qatar, and said that "people have been bullied by Max for years". Verstappen questioned the accuracy of Russell's claims and labelled him a "loser" and "backstabber".

The pair clashed once more on track at the 2025 Spanish Grand Prix when Verstappen, enraged at his own team for instructing him to let Russell through to avoid receiving a penalty, appeared to wave the Mercedes past before lunging into the side of it.

Verstappen was penalised by the stewards, later admitted the move was "not right" and apologised to his team, but did not personally address Russell.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Less talked about than the pair's clashes is a potential further tension added by Russell's boss Wolff having very publicly tried to sign Verstappen from Red Bull. Russell told Sky Sports F1 in June 2025 that his own contract extension was being delayed by Mercedes' attempts to sign Verstappen.

The previous clashes between the pair came when Russell was in a position of strength at Mercedes, given he had performed hugely impressively during his first four seasons with the team from 2022 to 2025.

Russell had expressed belief on many occasions over the years that if Mercedes delivered a title-winning car, he was ready to grab the opportunity, and few doubted him.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

However, when they finally produced such a car following the major regulation changes ahead of the 2026 season, it was his far less-experienced team-mate Antonelli who snatched away what Russell thought was going to be his title.

Russell has been tormented by his struggles throughout the season, repeatedly expressing uncertainty over what was causing his deficit to Antonelli before eventually appearing to decide that he must alter his driving style to be able to match the 20-year-old Italian in the sport's latest machinery.

If there was any doubt over how painful the season had been, it was crystalised by Wolff's decision to allow the Brit to leave the track in Mexico almost immediately after the race when Antonelli sealed the title, which the Austrian said was because he found Russell "distraught".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

It was one thing Russell 'standing up' to Verstappen when he could claim that given a strong car, he would rival the Dutchman, but the way the 2026 season has played out has left Russell vulnerable, a reality which Verstappen attempted to exploit with his "not on my level" remarks.

Not only has Russell been comprehensively outperformed by Antonelli, but he has now fallen to fifth in the drivers' standings, with Verstappen's four wins in the last six races having put him firmly on course for second place.

While Mercedes have proven in the past that they will allow both their drivers to fight for championships, there is no doubt that Antonelli has made himself the team's clear top dog for the tie being.

Given both championships have already been decided, the Russell-Verstappen feud is going to attract huge attention at the final two rounds of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

The best-case scenario for Russell across the season-ending triple header was to put together some strong results and enter the winter with some moment to take into 2027.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Verstappen, who has finished on the podium at nine successive races, and his own team-mate Antonelli, were always likely to be the biggest obstacles to that.

While Verstappen insisted in Las Vegas that he wasn't motivated by Russell's remarks, his comments on radio and after the race suggested there was some extra fire in his belly, which may well remain there in the Middle East.

The sporting challenge of claiming a victory may have stiffened, but Russell has also heightened his emotional load by putt himself back in the spotlight at a time where the relative calm offered by the titles having been decided may have been welcomed.

The drivers have in recent years established a tradition of all going for dinner one night at the final round in Abu Dhabi, where Verstappen famously offered Russell a seat next to him just days after their war of words in 2024.

While Russell won't want to completely back down after Verstappen's post-race comments in Las Vegas, a defusal of the situation might be the best thing for him.

Whether he takes that approach will become clear during Thursday's media sessions in Qatar, during which both drivers will speak to the press.

#759. How to make climate anxiety your superpower

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Download the Nature Podcast 23 November 2026

Late last week the UN’s climate conference, COP31, failed to reach a consensus on its headline message. That news came on the heels of the UN acknowledging that the 1.5 ˚C warming limit set out in Paris will be breached. So, it’s easy to feel anxious in a world where it seems that not enough is being done about climate change. But is it possible to overcome such anxiety or even use it?

In the final episode of Cooked? I open up about my own climate anxiety and discover that there are still things that I can do to battle climate change. And how those small individual actions could potentially lead to more systemic change.

00:00 Can I do anything about my climate anxiety?

04:43 What the science says about ‘ecoanxiety’

11:35 Can individuals really do anything?

Net zero emissions won’t reverse climate change — some nations look to ‘net negative’

The rise of eco-anxiety: scientists wake up to the mental-health toll of climate change

This episode was written and produced by Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was the editor. Music was by Akio Jefferson, Jonathan Maiocco, Aerial Circles, and Lionel Cohen, and was provided by Triple Scoop Music via Getty Images. Thanks to Emma Lawrance, Kimberly Nicholas, Madalina Vlasceanu and Elizabeth Howe for featuring in this episode.

Nick Petrić Howe: Hi mum, can you hear me okay?

Nick Petrić Howe: If you’ve been listening to this series, you’ll know that I’ve been struggling a bit with anxiety about the climate. If you’re just joining us now, hi, I’m Nick Petrić Howe and I have a climate anxiety problem. Throughout this series, I’ve spoken to a lot of scientists about the big ideas and big data that we can use to tackle climate change, but I haven’t really addressed the core reason of why I wanted to do this — to figure out what to do with my own feelings about climate change.

I wanted to know if I’d always felt this way, and if so, what I could do about it. So, I called up an expert on me. My mum.

Nick Petrić Howe: Can I record this call for work?

Elizabeth Howe: Yeah, course you can yeah

Nick Petrić Howe: Yeah? I just wanted to ask you something. When I was a kid, was I an anxious worried child would you say?

Nick Petrić Howe: This wasn’t exactly what I was expecting. I feel like I worry about things and have worried about them a lot throughout my life. But maybe there was something special about climate change, I know that it’s held a special position in my life. It’s why I decided to study biology when I finished school, eventually doing a PhD — to figure out if there was some way to help save the planet. So, I tried a different tack.

Nick Petrić Howe: Do you ever remember me worrying about, like, the environment and stuff. Elizabeth Howe: Oh God yeah. You were always thinking about stuff like that.

Elizabeth Howe: Well because you said— there was a big thing about climate change and you said ‘oh well climate change isn’t real because, you see, what happens is, in science, is that the world has these ice ages and then everything melts and then daa daa daa daaa.’ So you said, ‘it’s just a normal event, it’s not anything to do with global warming and it’s a load of rubbish.’ But you were always looking into stuff like that and listening to stuff like that. You were very interested in the scientific explanations for things.

Nick Petrić Howe: I’m not sure how I feel about that to be honest.

Nick Petrić Howe: Not gonna lie, being outed as a junior climate denier was not on my bingo card for this year. We eventually came to the conclusion that this was a phase I went through when I was quite young and hadn’t quite understood that people could just well… lie on national television. Misinformation, unfortunately, isn’t just a new thing. When I was a kid in the 90s, there were campaigns to make climate research seem a lot more questionable than now, and established politicians like Lord Nigel Lawson in the UK openly criticised the science.

At least, it seemed, I was interested in the climate. For the record, now I absolutely am convinced, along with the scientific community, that climate change is real and human caused.

And, even according to my mum, as I got older, I cared more about the climate, even if I wasn’t necessarily worried.

Elizabeth Howe: I don’t think you were particularly too worried…

Nick Petrić Howe: In fact, I remember thinking when I was a teenager and I was more appraised of the actual facts, that climate change was a solvable problem. One that my generation could fix. I was filled with notions of all the things that science had accomplished — the moon landings, the internet, and general relativity — breakthroughs that solved problems once thought insurmountable. It took me getting older to become a bit more jaded, concerned that we’d not done enough soon enough and that maybe it was too late.

But this got me thinking, if I wasn’t worried once and even felt hopeful. Is that something I could recapture? This series has already taught me that in many ways we’ve done more than I thought to tackle climate change and that people are actively working on solutions. But that only goes so far to assuage my own anxiety. So you’ll forgive me if I spend this episode figuring out if there’s something that can help me. Is there anything I can do?

Nick Petrić Howe: As I said, I’ve struggled with anxiety about climate change. Sometimes I feel paralysed by how hopeless it all seems. There’s so much to do and it’s not getting done fast enough. At the same time, every other week there seems to be another climate record smashed or a natural disaster exacerbated by climate change.

It’s easy to feel anxious. So, in this third and final episode of Cooked? I wanted to know - am I normal? Or am I bit of an outlier here? Are other people having these feelings of hopelessness in the face of climate change.

So, I called up one of the world experts on how climate change is affecting mental health.

Nick Petrić Howe: This is Emma Lawrance, from Imperial College London. After figuring out our settings, we connected on a slightly better line. And Emma told me that I’m by no means alone, in fact, it turns out there is a name for what I’m feeling. There’s a few actually.

Emma Lawrance: So there is this kind of emerging plethora of terms really that all centre on this kind of umbrella of what we might call psychological responses or emotional responses to the climate crisis. And so some of those terms can be things like climate related distress, climate anxiety, eco anxiety, ecological grief, solastalgia.

Nick Petrić Howe: And while there are differences between these terms, for the purposes of the podcast I’m just going to say eco-anxiety — the anxiety about climate change and environmental destruction, as that seems the most fitting with my experience.

And one of the first things that Emma impressed upon me is that there’s a lot we don’t know about eco-anxiety. This is a rapidly emerging field, but eco-anxiety is a thing that a lot of people are feeling. Especially if they’re dealing with the consequences of climate change.

Emma Lawrance: So for instance, in our sample of nearly 3,000 young people surveyed across the US, one fifth of the young people who didn't report experiencing a climate change-related event were afraid to have children that rose to one third of the young people who said they had already experienced a climate change-related event. And there was a correlation between the people sort of self-reporting and looking at their postcodes and where you know, climate hazards had been in the US. So, they seem to be kind of reflecting sort of a real-world experience.

Nick Petrić Howe: And that makes sense. If climate change is affecting you, then you would worry about it. I know my own anxiety spiked during the heatwaves, wildfires and droughts of this last British summer. But that does also mean that there are certain people who worry a bit more than others.

Emma Lawrance: There's more and more studies showing that eco-anxiety is definitely not like a white Western phenomenon. This experience of distress and what can be called eco-anxiety in response to changing climate is actually much higher in the countries and in the communities where these impacts are already occurring.

Nick Petrić Howe: That might surprise you, it certainly did me - In some ways, I had thought that maybe this was a worry more for people like me. Western, relatively well-off folks, who have time to worry about things. But, if my anxiety spiked over one record breaking summer, perhaps it shouldn’t be shocking that people facing these impacts week after week in the developing countries most effected, but least responsible for climate change are worried too. And they’re only getting more worried.

Emma Lawrance: It's happening in ways that are then compounding. So people are experiencing not just one, but multiple kind of stresses and disasters, often coming back-to-back and they're not having time to recover before the next one hits that experience into place with this awareness of, well, what's to come? The awareness of the injustice of the situation of often kind of insufficient climate action and power dynamics between, you know, the people who are affected and the people causing the problem and growing inequalities in some spaces or many spaces globally. those things are we're seeing this really rapid increase in the use of the term eco anxiety. So I think there's over a 4,000-fold percent increase in Google searches. five-year period. And so, it’s really skyrocketed

Nick Petrić Howe: Strangely, it feels a little better to know that I’m not alone in these feelings. Perhaps I am a bit more normal than I thought. But I wanted to know what could be done about these feelings. For me, the anxiety has sometimes been paralysing. I haven’t wanted to engage with climate news, which, as I’ve said, is a bit of a funny position to be in as a science journalist. And Emma explained to me that, for some people it can be like that. It can even affect people’s daily lives, and those people may need some extra help and support, but for many people this anxiety can be quite an understandable reaction.

Emma Lawrance: Eco-anxiety isn't something that the vast majority of researchers and people living with these experiences and profession and, mental health professionals would say needs to be a quote unquote, like diagnosis. And it's something that is, can be very rational. It's understandable, and often proportionate to feel alarm, to feel distressed, to feel the strong emotions in response to the facts of the climate crisis.

Nick Petrić Howe: And for some people, it may even be a feeling they want to hold onto. They can use it to push them to battle climate change.

Emma Lawrance: We also know that people who are feeling that distress are more likely to be taking pro-environmental action. We know that collective action, particularly rather than individual action can help you like hold high distress and protect your mental health and wellbeing. it's not sometimes holding distress can impact, you know, is related to poorer mental health, it's related to higher insomnia, et cetera. But young people are saying, you know, we don't want our distress to be taken away in a sense, because this shows that we care. It shows that we care about the world. It can be fuel for action, but that action needs to be often done with others. And also can for some people lead into action that ends up providing more meaning and joy and purpose and it can be a really good thing, but for others it can be overwhelming and paralysing and have really severe impacts on their life

Nick Petrić Howe: So, to my question of what I’m supposed to do with these feelings... I think I’m already doing it. These feelings can overwhelm, and I’ve certainly felt that. But maybe doing something is a way to help live with these anxious feelings. The question is though, what do you do?

Kimberly Nicholas: I really think if your listeners were taking these high-impact climate actions just 20 minutes a day. It would be enough.

Nick Petrić Howe: Now, what I don't want to do is make you feel as though the weight of the world is on your shoulders. Saying that you are ultimately responsible for climate change is too much of a burden for any one person to bear. As someone who worries a lot, I think that weight would crush me, frankly. It’s also fair to say that many of these problems are systemic too. Governments, nations, and businesses should all meet ambitious climate targets if we’re to avoid the worst consequences of climate change. And if you live in the US, say, even if you have very minimal emissions compared to your neighbours, you’re likely to have higher emissions than someone in Bangladesh — just because of how baked in carbon emissions are. If you have an electric car in the US, for example, it’s getting electricity from more fossil fuel power plants than someone in Norway. So, it’s easy to think that any individual action is a waste of time.

Kimberly Nicholas: Well, ineffective individual actions are a waste of time.

Nick Petrić Howe: This is Kimberly Nicholas, a climate scientist at Lund University. And she’s someone who’s spent quite a bit of time thinking about what individuals can do, and perhaps what they shouldn’t do.

Kimberly Nicholas: We don't need to focus on recycling or canvas bags. People really have the wrong ideas about what individual action means. And so that I think is a myth that we need to dispel. So, it's not about doing everything, it's not that every little thing matters, it's that focusing our limited time and energy where it can really make a difference can lead us to take powerful actions today that do lead to system change.

Nick Petrić Howe: And it’s not just the what that Kimberly has been thinking about, it’s the who too.

Kimberly Nicholas: I really focus on this group that is in the top 10% globally, many of whom are surprised to learn that they are in that group. So if you earn over about 38,000 US dollars or 35,000 euros a year, your income is in the top 10% globally. And that group produces about half of household carbon pollution and also has enormous political, economic, cultural power.

Nick Petrić Howe: I was among those surprised to find myself in that group. Being in the 10% of income doesn’t quite gel with my, admittedly comfortable, but fairly ordinary life. It’s worth saying as well, that power and carbon emissions track income as it rises too. With around a fifth of warming between 1990 and 2020 attributable to people in the top 1% of income, and a bit under a tenth to those in the top 0.1%.

But the top 10%, which I’m going to guess includes a lot of you listening, still have a lot that they can do, according to Kimberly. She notes that things like reducing air travel, investing in low-emission funds, and switching to renewable energy providers could be effective. She’s even created a guide for people online where you can find what the highest impact climate actions you personally can take. She calls it finding your superpower.

Now, there are researchers who are critical of these ideas. Arguing that individual actions, like these, are a distraction from larger more systemic changes that should be taking place. And others have argued that the fossil fuel industry has used individual actions to take onus off themselves. In fact, carbon footprints — which focus on the emissions of an individual — were popularised by the fossil fuel industry.

But I spoke to a lot of different experts for this series, and they mostly agreed on both being important. We’ll need individual actions and systemic changes. And one doesn’t preclude the other. Things like individual actions may also actually lead to bigger changes.

This is also why Kimberly focuses on specific actions that she feels will have the biggest impacts. And one key one for those who live in a liberal democracy, where you can freely vote for your leaders, is to try and use your individual power to lead to systemic change.

Kimberly Nicholas: For those of us who do live in those countries, we have incredible powers like voting and encouraging and getting others to vote, mobilizing voting, joining a political party or organization that's taking powerful climate action. And the reason those types of actions are so important is that climate policies that affect everyone in a society, of course, have enormous potential, far bigger than, you know, our everyday lives at home, to really move the needle and dramatically decrease climate pollution.

Nick Petrić Howe: And it’s not just politics. This could also be things like engaging with climate action at work. Many workplaces have climate goals and there are usually other keen people you can connect with to try and make these goals happen. Maybe your own climate efforts are small, but a company of 10, 100 or thousands of people could make a much more tangible difference.

For example, there has been an employee-led effort to urge their companies to leave the US Chamber of Commerce. This business association rejected the scientific consensus on climate change until 2019 and has historically obstructed climate action. More recently, it has acknowledged that humans contribute to climate change, however, it still lobbied against the Inflation Reduction Act. So, climate concerned employees of the companies that are members of the Chamber have been petitioning their firms to leave the organisation. Many of those companies have now objected to the Chamber’s climate policies.

In fact, when I spoke to Kimberly it seemed that a lot of the ‘individual’ actions she suggested were really about connecting to others, be that political organising or simply socialising with other climate-conscious people. Those actions could build to something more, but they could also help with the reason I started this podcast in the first place. Anxiety.

Kimberly Nicholas: We want to make climate action fun. It should be something we look forward to and enjoy doing. That's one of the best parts of our week. and we know that from research, doing things together in community helps prevent burnout, it can help reduce anxiety, it can help motivate us and keep us going. And we all have ups and downs. I mean, we've all had moments of despair working on the climate crisis is not an easy thing to do. but we've also had moments of incredible elation and connection and creativity and joy. So being able to be in community is really powerful.

Nick Petrić Howe: And it could be that by connecting people together, that could ultimately lead to societal change.

Madalina Vlasceanu: I think there's this positive feedback loop by which all of our individual level actions can lead to bigger collective actions. And then collective actions can then trigger system level changes. The system level changes can then make it easier for individuals to take additional individual level actions because they would ideally remove the barriers to action.

Nick Petrić Howe: I have to admit that after my chat with Kimberley, I certainly felt a bit more empowered, but I was still a bit sceptical about the power of individuals. It’s not that I think individuals can’t do anything, it’s just the scale of the challenge that makes me hesitate. Even if I am, or even everyone listening is, the most climate conscious warriors in the world, it probably wouldn’t be enough. Like Kimberley alluded to, those individuals actions need to build towards the systemic. We need to change society.

I was curious about what the research said about the connection between the individual and the systemic and importantly, how can we actually get these small actions to help battle the global problem of climate change. So, I called up Madalina Vlasceanu, a social scientist who’s thought a lot about this exact issue.

Madalina Vlasceanu: So in my work we think about what are some ways in which collective action can be triggered at the individual level and then spread and catalyzed around groups and then collectives and then eventually making some system level pro changes.

Nick Petrić Howe: In our chat, one of the things that Madalina impressed upon me is that, while she believes that individual actions can lead to collective ones and then to systemic change, there are barriers that we need to acknowledge. For example, if you think the transition to renewable energy, the big barrier there is that fossil fuels are hugely subsidised. According to the International Monetary Fund, in 2024 fossil fuel subsidies were around $725 billion worldwide. If the underpricing of environmental costs are taken into account, such as air pollution and their contribution to climate change, that number rises to $6.7 trillion. In either case, fossil fuels are being made cheaper than they should be, which is not ideal when we should be using less of them.

Madalina Vlasceanu: So, our energy system needs to change and this can only happen through laws, policies, regulations that reduce, for example, fossil fuel subsidies currently valued at trillions of dollars. And in order for this to happen, for these systemic regulations to be introduced and enforced, there needs to, of course, be massive awareness campaigns from the public. So the public can push in this direction and make this direction the normative direction. So there is a big component here of the transition that has to do with laws, but the laws will likely change as an effect of pressure from the public.

Nick Petrić Howe: In fact, one reason that these subsidies persist is due to perceived unpopularity of raising the prices of fossil fuels — even if a switch to renewables would be cheaper in the long term. You may well have seen how people react to increases in heating or petrol costs. So, for politicians to make such changes, they’d need to believe that the public is on their side. Which is actually a strange position to be in, as most people do think that climate change is a big problem.

Research and polls show that the majority of people worldwide support climate action. So why do policymakers need convincing? Well, the problem is that support on a poll doesn’t necessarily translate to action.

Madalina Vlasceanu: There is a big difference between being aware of the problem in principle and being aware of this problem viscerally at a level where you know it's affecting you personally. So we know people have an optimism bias. and even though intellectually they can conceptualize that, well, there is this problem, people are talking about it, scientists are in agreement, it is going to get worse. And we understand that. At the same time, two things can be true. And so what is also true is that people think, well, this is probably not gonna affect me, or at least not very soon. And this is the type of thing where it'll probably happen first somewhere really far away or to other people or sometime in the pretty distant future. So I'd rather spend today or the near future thinking about more immediate issues that I have to worry about.

Nick Petrić Howe: I can certainly relate to spending my time worrying about things other than climate change. So, how do you actually get people to act? Madalina’s research has revealed some clues. By testing different interventions on a sample of 30,000 US citizens, she and a team of researchers were able to see what could actually get people to collectively act on climate change.

Madalina Vlasceanu: The top intervention leveraged two processes. So the two processes are efficacy beliefs and positive emotions. So efficacy beliefs means the belief that engaging in this activity will actually pay off in the exact way in which you're hoping it will. So the belief that if I do attend this protest, this protest will then reduce the risk of climate change. And so the way in which you can achieve this efficacy belief induction is by giving people examples of times in which such participation in collective action has actually had meaningful effects.

Nick Petrić Howe: Such examples include the banning of fossil fuel extraction in Quebec due to decades of grassroots movements and Los Angeles moving to ban urban oil extraction, because of years of protests and community organising.

Madalina Vlasceanu: And the other process I mentioned is positive emotions. So in addition to feeling like you will make a difference, you also need to feel like there is an emotional benefit to you personally, not just to the cause of the participation. So meaning-making, increasing belonging, or starting some close relationships with like-minded others. All of these more personal motivations to engage in collective action are also critical to engagement.

Nick Petrić Howe: Madalina also found that appealing to ideas like preserving the purity of the environment and respect for authority can also encourage more action — and these interventions were effective across the political spectrum.

To encourage more action, these interventions could be employed by governments, NGOs, charities and people making podcasts... They could say that you can make a difference, and you may even make some friends along the way. And by encouraging people to get together and act on climate, Madalina thinks we can create a positive feedback loop where more climate action is done, which makes it easier for us all to do more climate action.

Madalina Vlasceanu: It could be, for example, that someone's very motivated to not pollute very much or not use a lot of fossil fuels, but the system doesn't necessarily facilitate these actions. So it makes it much harder for me as an individual not to pollute, even if I wanted to. And so if I participate in collective action to change some of those systemic level decisions then it could be even easier for me to engage in individual level climate action by having an easier time engaging in in individual level behavioural change, such as you know, engaging in ways of transport that are less polluting.

If you’re sceptical about the power of groups of people, then we can take lessons from historical changes of the past. During the civil rights movement in the US, collections of small groups came together and organised protests, civil disobedience and boycotts that eventually led to new civil rights laws and the end of most legal discrimation against African Americans.

Madalina Vlasceanu: the main thing an individual can do to address climate change is to be less of an individual. And so we have to recognize the power in groups in the power of our collective to making change.

Nick Petrić Howe: So, if you want to fight climate change. Remember this. You can make a change, people have done it before, and it may even be good for you to do so.

Madalina Vlasceanu: Hopelessness is pretty natural, I would say. I felt hopelessness quite a lot at the beginning of this journey when I was first becoming aware of just how big the threat is. especially when I became a mother and I understood that my kids will inherit a very different world and a much worse one. Than I had. And so hopelessness is there. the one way I found to cope or to get out of it is by taking action. So action is the antidote to hopelessness.

Nick Petrić Howe: In this podcast series, I wanted to find out if there was anything I could do about climate change. And it turns out that perhaps things are not as bad as I thought. There are certainly challenges, and some big unknowns as to what might happen in the future.

But as humans, we have a tendency to focus on the negative. And when it comes to climate change, there’s plenty of negative to think about. Even if things are not as bad as I thought, we’re not really on track to meet our climate targets. We need more action, but perhaps that’s something in which we all have a role to play.

And according to the science, we can make a difference. I’m certainly trying to. [Since starting this podcast, I’ve changed my pension to be invested in climate-conscious way, joined a group organising for climate action in my company, and started talking more to people about climate. I’m talking to you right now. And that’s helped, with my anxiety. I just hope that it helps with the world.]

In the end, I turned my climate anxiety, into what I hope is a climate superpower — I’m still anxious but I’m using that energy to push me, to try and make difference. As Madalina said, Action is the antidote to hopelessness. I hope I’ve helped you feel a bit less hopeless.

For now, I’ll leave you with a final quote from Madalina.

Nick Petrić Howe: And then my last question is: how do we save the world?

Madalina Vlasceanu: Haha, good question. In my mind how we save the world is caring about each other and helping each other out.

Nick Petrić Howe: This podcast series was written and produced by me, Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was my editor. Thanks also to Emma Lawrance, Kimberly Nicholas, Madalina Vlasceanu, and, of course, my mum for talking to me for this episode. And thank you all for listening too. If you like this sort of thing, then Kimberly has got her own climate podcast, I’ll link to that in the show notes as well.
